required_facts_checked: SQLiteSearch targets small personal and course projects as a persistent local middle ground between minsearch and infrastructure-heavy systems.
Requirements were Python availability, easy setup, local execution without Docker and text plus vector search.
Elasticsearch was aimed at large production systems and described as costing more than $200 per month; Qdrant and PostgreSQL would require an external service or Docker in this use case.
minsearch had a simple text-and-vector API but stored its index in memory, losing data when the Python process ended.
SQLite provided embedded local text search and persistence but no vector search by default.
lshashing kept hash tables in memory, SparseLSH lacked SQLite support and narrow-down used a native Rust extension.
The implementation used locality-sensitive hashing based on random projections familiar to Alexey.
The API was designed to resemble minsearch for Buildcamp participants.
ChatGPT researched and planned the design, Claude Code read plan.md and implemented it, and tests were requested.
The project began as LightSearch and was renamed SQLiteSearch because litesearch was already taken on PyPI.
The final index stores data tables, lookup structures and metadata in one SQLite file without a separate server.
The /release command automates package publication and can rerun after Claude diagnoses build or test failures.
unsupported_claims_removed: Removed claims about benchmark performance, universal scalability or guaranteed search quality not stated in the source.
Removed claims that would turn the small-project recommendation into a general replacement for production search systems.
substantive_edits: Rewrote the article as a reader-facing explanation organized around requirements, candidate evaluation, LSH, architecture and release.
Preserved the reasons each alternative failed and the distinction between persistent local search and large infrastructure.
Explained the ChatGPT-to-Claude Code handoff without attributing independent design decisions to the tools.
